config.title: forwardRef & Exposing DOM Nodes

intro.title: forwardRef & Exposing DOM Nodes
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Angular component that uses a button to focus on a text input field. You will learn how to use forwardRef to resolve circular dependencies when accessing a component's template reference. The core concept is exposing DOM nodes to the parent component using Angular's ElementRef and ViewChild decorators. You'll work with TypeScript, template references, and event binding to connect the button click to the input focus. By the end, you'll understand how to safely reference and control DOM elements within an Angular application.
intro.usecase: In real applications, forwardRef and DOM node exposure are essential when building reusable form components with complex validation logic. For example, in enterprise dashboards with data tables, you might create a custom filter panel component that needs direct access to specific input fields for focus management or validation state. This pattern also appears in interactive UI libraries where modal dialogs or dropdown menus require programmatic control over their trigger elements. Developers use these techniques to create maintainable component APIs that allow parent components to interact with child DOM elements without breaking encapsulation.

objectives: Apply forwardRef to resolve circular dependency issues in component references
Construct a component that exposes its DOM node using ElementRef
Configure a parent component to access a child component's DOM node via ViewChild
Implement a method that manipulates the exposed DOM node's properties
Initialize a template reference variable to bind to a child component
Update a parent component's view by controlling the child's exposed DOM element
Integrate forwardRef with ViewChild to access component instances before initialization

steps.title: Import Component, forwardRef, and ElementRef from Angular core
steps.instruction: Import Component, forwardRef, and ElementRef from '@angular/core'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import multiple symbols from the same module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing multiple Angular core APIs
import { Component, OnInit } from '@angular/core';
steps.seedCode: // Import Component, forwardRef, and ElementRef from '@angular/core'
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports for Component, forwardRef, and ElementRef are added at the top of the file.
successCriteria: Component, forwardRef, and ElementRef are imported from '@angular/core'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but make sure you're importing all three symbols: Component, forwardRef, and ElementRef from '@angular/core'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. You need to import Component, forwardRef, and ElementRef from '@angular/core'.

steps.title: Create a child component with forwardRef
steps.instruction: Define a child component class named 'ChildComponent' decorated with @Component. The component's template should contain a button element with the text 'Click me'.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator to define the component. The template can be a simple string with a button element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ChildComponent class is created with a button in its template, ready to accept a forwardRef in the next step.
successCriteria: ChildComponent class is defined with @Component decorator and a template containing a button element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the component has both the @Component decorator and a template with a button.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Check that you used @Component and included a button in the template.

steps.title: Add ElementRef injection to the child component
steps.instruction: In your ChildComponent class, add a constructor that injects ElementRef and stores it in a property.
steps.hint: Use the constructor parameter to inject ElementRef and assign it to a class property.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: injecting a service
constructor(private elementRef: ElementRef) {}
steps.expectedOutcome: The ChildComponent will have a constructor that injects ElementRef, making the component's native DOM element accessible.
successCriteria: Constructor is added with ElementRef injection and stored in a property.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're injecting ElementRef in the constructor and storing it properly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constructor injection for ElementRef is missing or incorrect. Check the syntax for dependency injection in Angular.

steps.title: Create a parent component
steps.instruction: Define a parent component class named ParentComponent with the @Component decorator and a basic template that will contain the child component.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator with a selector like 'app-parent' and a template that includes the child component selector.
steps.expectedOutcome: A parent component class is created with a basic template structure, ready to host the child component.
successCriteria: ParentComponent class is defined with @Component decorator, a selector, and a template containing the child component selector.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the parent component has a selector and a template that includes the child component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The parent component definition is missing or incomplete. Ensure you define a class with @Component decorator and a template.

steps.title: Add ViewChild to the parent component
steps.instruction: In the parent component, add a ViewChild property named 'childRef' that references the ChildComponent instance.
steps.hint: Use the @ViewChild decorator with the ChildComponent type. This will allow the parent to access the child component's properties and methods.
steps.expectedOutcome: The parent component will have a ViewChild property that can reference the child component instance.
successCriteria: ParentComponent has a ViewChild property named 'childRef' with type ChildComponent.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added the ViewChild decorator with the correct type and property name.
steps.feedbackWrong: The parent component doesn't have a ViewChild property yet. Remember to use @ViewChild(ChildComponent) with a property name like 'childRef'.

steps.title: Add template reference variable to child in parent template
steps.instruction: In the parent component's template, add a template reference variable named #childRef to the child component selector.
steps.hint: Template reference variables start with # and are placed on the element tag in the template.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a template reference variable to an element
<app-child #childRef></app-child>
steps.expectedOutcome: The parent component's template now contains the child component with a template reference variable that can be used with ViewChild.
successCriteria: The template reference variable is named #childRef
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a template reference variable, but check the name or syntax. It should be #childRef on the <app-child> element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template reference variable is missing or incorrect. Add #childRef to the <app-child> element in the parent template.

steps.title: Implement click handler to access child's DOM node
steps.instruction: In the ParentComponent class, create a method named 'logChildElement' that accesses the child's ElementRef and logs the native DOM element to the console.
steps.hint: Inside the method, you can access the child's native element using this.childRef.nativeElement and then log it with console.log().
steps.expectedOutcome: The ParentComponent will have a method that can access and log the child component's native DOM element when called.
successCriteria: The ParentComponent class contains a method named 'logChildElement' that accesses the child's native element and logs it to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a method, but it doesn't yet access the child's native element. Make sure to use the ViewChild reference to get the ElementRef and then access its nativeElement property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The method isn't implemented correctly. Remember to create a method named 'logChildElement' in the ParentComponent class that accesses the child's native DOM element.

steps.title: Wire the button click to the handler
steps.instruction: In the parent component's template, bind the button's click event to the logChildElement method using Angular's event binding syntax.
steps.hint: Use parentheses around the event name (like (click)) and set it equal to the method name with parentheses.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: binding a button click to a handler
<button (click)="handleClick()">Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The parent component's template will have a button that, when clicked, triggers the logChildElement method to access the child's DOM node.
successCriteria: The parent template contains a button with (click)="logChildElement()" event binding.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using Angular's event binding syntax with parentheses around 'click' and calling the method with parentheses.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button click isn't properly wired to the handler. Remember to use (click)="logChildElement()" in the parent template.

steps.title: Test the DOM node access
steps.instruction: Run the application and click the button to see the child component's DOM element logged to the console
steps.hint: Make sure your development server is running, open the browser console, and click the button in the parent component.
steps.analogousExample:
// Testing component functionality
console.log('Component is working correctly');
steps.expectedOutcome: When you click the 'Log Child DOM' button, you should see the child component's DOM element logged in the browser console.
successCriteria: The application runs without errors and clicking the button logs the child component's DOM element to the console
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: The application runs but the DOM element isn't logged. Check that your button click handler is properly implemented and the ViewChild reference is correctly set up.
steps.feedbackWrong: The application doesn't run or the button doesn't work. Review your component setup, template bindings, and ViewChild configuration.
